sweep_summary: Three title-hits for nama1264. (1) Selting 1995 is a false Glottolog language assignment (record says 'computerized assignment from gesprach'); it is a book on German conversational prosody — irrelevant, not downloaded. (2) Kusmer 2019 (already held by the project, re-read) is about tone sandhi and prosodic displacement; silent on word stress. (3) Brugman 2009, downloaded open from Cornell eCommons (hdl 1813/13921, 321 pp., saved with extracted text), is the key find: p.28 'Khoekhoe lacks both stress and segmental alternations' and p.88 'Khoekhoe has no stress, segment or tone alternations' — a first-hand, fieldwork-based statement that CONTRADICTS the catalog's fixed-strict (initial) coding, which currently has no located source text and rests on Gordon 2002's appendix line 'Initial (mora)' (via Hagman 1977). Earlier files held by the project add Hahn 1870 §8 p.24 (accent on the monosyllabic stem = first syllable) and Planert 1905 p.109 (stress sometimes on stem, sometimes on suffix; 'Die Ansicht Fr. Müllers über die Betonung ist also nicht richtig'). Net: sources conflict; the best modern statement is 'no stress'. Still unread and worth acquiring: Hagman 1977 Nama Hottentot grammar (print only; Google Books API 0 items, HathiTrust catalog behind an automated-access block, archive.org 0 hits) — high priority as the StressTyp2/Gordon source; Beach 1938 and Haacke 1999 tonology medium.

new_statements.reading: A modern, fieldwork-based phonological study states outright that Khoekhoe (Nama) has no word stress; word-level prominence is tonal (six citation melodies, left-aligned) and structural (bimoraic root = head foot), not metrical stress. This is the first explicit first-hand statement on the question read for this language and it contradicts the catalog's fixed-strict initial coding. It also conflicts with Hahn 1870 §8 p.24 ('Der Accent bleibt auf der Stammsilbe.. stets auf der ersten Silbe'), an 1870 statement whose 'Accent' sits beside a three-way tone description (§7), and Planert 1905 p.109 already contradicted Hahn ('betont bald die Stammsilbe, bald das Suffix'). The catalog entry should move from fixed-strict to at least 'descriptions disagree', and to no word stress/tonal if Hagman 1977 (unread; the Gordon 2002 source) does not give an explicit stress rule.

new_statements.quote: § 8. Der Accent bleibt auf der Stammsilbe, und, da — wie weiter unten in der Wortbildungslehre gezeigt werden soll — alle Stämme des Wortes im Hottentotischen monosyllabisch sind, stets auf der ersten Silbe. Bei Compositen aus Stoffwörtern fällt der Ton dagegen auf diejenige erste Silbe der Wurzel, welche den Begriff des zusammengesetzten Wortes hauptsächlich bestimmt. Z. B. gáo-ao-b (gao herrschen, ao etwas vorstellen, b Suffix masc.) d. h. König. [...] In reduplicirten Stämmen hat in der Regel die erste Silbe den Ton, |nám — |nam lieben; tritt jedoch ein adjectivisches oder adverbiales Suffix an den Namen so geht der Ton auf die zweite Silbe über z. B. |nam — |nám — sa, liebenswürdig.
new_statements.translation: § 8. The accent stays on the stem syllable, and, since — as will be shown below in the word-formation section — all word stems in Hottentot are monosyllabic, always on the first syllable. In compounds of content words, by contrast, the accent (Ton) falls on the first syllable of that root which chiefly determines the meaning of the compound word. E.g. gáo-ao-b (gao 'to rule', ao 'to represent something', b masc. suffix), i.e. 'king'. [...] In reduplicated stems the first syllable as a rule carries the accent, |nám-|nam 'to love'; but if an adjectival or adverbial suffix is attached to the noun the accent passes to the second syllable, e.g. |nam-|nám-sa 'lovable'.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's fixed: initial syllable coding (initial stress). Contradicts the existing Brugman 2009 statement (Khoekhoe has no stress) and is already contradicted by Planert 1905 p.109 (accent sometimes on stem, sometimes on suffix). Hahn's 'Accent' stands next to his three-tone description and he alternates 'Accent'/'Ton' within § 8, so the 1870 statement is weak evidence for metrical stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent sits on the (monosyllabic) stem, hence on the first syllable of the word; in compounds it goes to the initial syllable of the semantically dominant root; reduplicated stems are initial-accented unless an adjectival/adverbial suffix is added, in which case the accent moves to the second syllable. Note that § 7 immediately before describes a three-way lexical tone (Tiefton/Mittelton/Hochton) and § 8 uses 'Accent' and 'Ton' interchangeably, so it is not certain that Hahn's 'Accent' is metrical stress rather than tonal prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds: accent on the first syllable of the root that chiefly determines the compound's meaning (gáo-ao-b 'king', Tsũ-||góab). Reduplicated stems with an adjectival or adverbial suffix: accent shifts to the second syllable (|nam-|nám-sa).
new_statements.identity_note: All works opened describe Nama/Namaqua Hottentot (Khoekhoe) as spoken in Namaqualand / Great Namaqualand in the mid-19th century (Tindall: Wesleyan mission Namaqua; Hahn: Nama, with Sprachproben). Peters 1972 concerns place names of Ngamiland (north-western Botswana) and, unread, cannot be confirmed to describe Nama at all. Catalog record 'Tindall n.d.' and 'Tindall 1857' are the same book.

tone_statements.citation: Haacke, Wilfrid [Heinrich] [Gerhard] (1992). The tonology of Khoekhoe (Nama/Damara). Köln: Köppe. University College London. 233 pp.
tone_statements.quote: It has been shown that lexical tone in Khoekhoe is based on a bimoraic foot, and that each melody must be analyzed in terms of two tonemes out of a set of four. An analysis of these tones in terms of a HIGH and a LOW tone feature on one tier, and a UPPER REGISTER feature on another, i.a. permits an account of the Flip-flop rule, as well as of a tono- genetic split in Khoekhoe, according to which three original tonemes split into six through the influence of depressor consonants. For practical purposes only four’ surface tonemes need to be recognized, however, bacause of partial overlap.
tone_statements.locator: p. 266, ch. 5 'Conclusion'; supporting: sec. 2.1.2 pp. 27-28 (four tonemes Double-Low/Low/High/Double-High; 't.b.u. is coextensive with the syllable'), sec. 2.2.2 pp. 73-76, sec. 2.3 pp. 140-141
tone_statements.summary: Register system: four level tonemes (Double-Low, Low, High, Double-High) combine two per bimoraic root into six major melodies with sandhi and flip-flop alternants; contours are level sequences.

readall_conflicts: The sources disagree on whether Nama has word stress at all. Hahn 1870 § 8 (p.24) says the accent stays on the monosyllabic stem and therefore always on the first syllable (with compound and suffix exceptions), which is the placement the catalog records (via Gordon 2002 / Hagman 1977, unread). Planert 1905 p.109 (read in an earlier search) already rejected that rule: accent falls now on the stem, now on the suffix. Brugman 2009 (existing statement, pp.28, 88), a modern fieldwork phonology, states that Khoekhoe has no stress and that word prominence is tonal. Tindall 1857 (both copies) mentions accented syllables only as the locus of vowel length and gives no placement. Hahn's own text weakens his statement as evidence for metrical stress: § 7 describes a three-way lexical tone and § 8 uses 'Accent' and 'Ton' as synonyms. Peters 1972 could not be opened.

tone.quote: It has been shown that lexical tone in Khoekhoe is based on a bimoraic foot, and that each melody must be analyzed in terms of two tonemes out of a set of four. An analysis of these tones in terms of a HIGH and a LOW tone feature on one tier, and a UPPER REGISTER feature on another, i.a. permits an account of the Flip-flop rule, as well as of a tono- genetic split in Khoekhoe, according to which three original tonemes split into six through the influence of depressor consonants. For practical purposes only four’ surface tonemes need to be recognized, however, bacause of partial overlap.
tone.locator: p. 266, ch. 5 'Conclusion'; supporting: sec. 2.1.2 pp. 27-28 (four tonemes Double-Low/Low/High/Double-High; 't.b.u. is coextensive with the syllable'), sec. 2.2.2 pp. 73-76, sec. 2.3 pp. 140-141
tone.summary: Register system: four level tonemes (Double-Low, Low, High, Double-High) combine two per bimoraic root into six major melodies with sandhi and flip-flop alternants; contours are level sequences.

tone.quote: Noteworthy is the alternation between former depressor releases and non-depressor releases, particularly Xh (depressor) with Xkh (non-depressor). A systematic study of any possible influence of this alternation on the tonology has not yet been undertaken. … In the case of egressive consonants, however, the effect on tonemes was the opposite: kh consistently was a depressor … The letters p/b, t/d, k/d all represent voiceless stops and are used distinctively merely to indicate ligher and lower tones respectively.
